text: Windows gives you drive letters — C colon, D colon. Linux has no concept of one — everything, no matter how many disks or network mounts sit behind it, hangs off a single tree starting at the root directory, and nearly every distro lays that tree out the same way, thanks to a shared convention called the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard.

A listing of the root directory on almost any Linux box looks the same: etc, var, home, usr, bin, opt, tmp, and root, each with its own well-defined job. Learn this map once, and you can navigate a server you've never touched before, because the pieces are always roughly in the same place no matter whose server it is.

/etc holds system-wide configuration — nearly every service reads its settings from somewhere under here. /var holds data that changes constantly: logs, mail queues, caches. /home holds each regular user's personal directory. /usr holds the bulk of the actual installed software, not /bin.

/bin holds the essential command binaries you need even in recovery mode — ls, cp, cat — usually symlinked into /usr/bin on modern distros. /opt holds optional, self-contained third-party software. /tmp holds temporary files any process can write, routinely wiped on reboot. And /root is the root user's own home directory — not the same thing as the / root directory itself.

Of all of it, /var/log is the directory you'll open most. Syslog, or messages on Red Hat-family systems, is the general system log — the first thing worth checking when something breaks and you don't yet know what. Individual services like nginx or mysql usually get their own subdirectory underneath.

That's the whole point of a shared standard: a bug report telling you to check the config or find the crash evidence already tells you exactly where to look, on any distro. Next up: the actual commands you'll use to move around that tree — ls, cd, cp, mv, rm, grep, and find.
